title: Shared responsibility by cloud model
prompt: A company runs workloads on IaaS, PaaS and SaaS offerings from a public cloud provider. Under the shared responsibility model, classify who is responsible for each task.

items.text: IaaS: patching the VM's guest OS
items.why: In IaaS the customer manages everything from the OS up, including patching.
The virtualization layer is part of the provider's infrastructure in every model.

items.text: PaaS: patching the managed runtime and OS
items.why: In PaaS the provider runs the platform (OS, runtime, middleware).

items.text: PaaS: fixing flaws in the app code you deploy
items.why: The customer always owns the code it writes and deploys on a platform.
In SaaS the provider runs the entire application stack.

items.text: SaaS: granting and revoking user access
items.why: Even in SaaS, the customer manages its own users, permissions and data.
Facilities, hardware and physical access are always the provider's job.

explanation: The provider's share grows from IaaS to PaaS to SaaS. IaaS: provider owns facilities, hardware and hypervisor; the customer owns OS, apps and data. PaaS: the provider also owns the OS and runtime; the customer owns its code and data. SaaS: the provider owns the whole application; the customer still owns its data, identities and access configuration. A responsibility matrix in the contract should spell out the split.

title: Data states: at rest, in transit, in use
prompt: A data protection officer is mapping where customer records exist so the right protection can be applied to each. Classify each situation by the state of the data.

items.text: Database files on an encrypted SAN volume
items.why: Stored on media and not actively moving or being processed: at rest.

items.text: Backup tapes kept in an offsite vault
items.why: Archived on storage media: at rest.
Moving across the network between client and server: in transit.

items.text: Site-to-site replication over an IPsec tunnel
items.why: Crossing a network link between locations: in transit.

items.text: Record loaded into app memory for processing
items.why: Decrypted in RAM while the application works on it: in use.

items.text: Values in CPU registers during a calculation
items.why: Actively being processed by the CPU: in use.

explanation: Data at rest is stored (disks, databases, backups) and is protected with full-disk, volume, database or file encryption plus permissions. Data in transit moves across a network and is protected with TLS, IPsec or VPNs. Data in use sits in memory or CPU while being processed and is the hardest to protect; secure enclaves and trusted execution environments address it.

title: Resilience requirements and strategies
prompt: A CIO lists resilience requirements for several systems. Match each requirement to the strategy that BEST meets it.

pairs.left: Fail over in minutes with live replicated data
pairs.why: A hot site is fully equipped and kept in sync, so operations can move almost immediately.

pairs.left: Some gear ready; restore backups in hours to days
pairs.why: A warm site has hardware and connectivity but needs current data loaded before it can take over.

pairs.left: Lowest cost; space and power only
pairs.why: A cold site is an empty facility; equipment must be delivered and configured, so recovery is slowest.

pairs.left: One regional disaster must not hit both sites
pairs.why: Placing sites far apart keeps a single flood, storm or grid failure from affecting both.

pairs.left: One provider outage must not stop service
pairs.why: Running across more than one cloud provider removes dependence on a single provider.

pairs.left: One OS flaw must not affect every server
pairs.why: Using different operating systems or platforms means one vulnerability cannot compromise them all.

explanation: Site types trade cost for recovery speed: hot is fastest and most expensive, cold is cheapest and slowest, and warm sits between. The other strategies remove a single point of failure at a different layer: location (geographic dispersion), provider (multi-cloud) and technology (platform diversity).
